title: Are You Solving the Problem for Your Child or Replacing the Skill
author: Playful Brains
summary: This piece diagnoses a recurring pattern in family life where well-intentioned parental intervention, checking the backpack every night, stepping in to speak for an anxious child, produces visible short-term relief but no durable improvement in the child's own capability. Its central distinction is between an outcome (the backpack gets packed) and the underlying capacity that outcome depends on (remembering a future task, sequencing steps, noticing what's missing, operating a system independently), arguing that parents who fix only the outcome inadvertently make the developmental work disappear even as the immediate crisis resolves. The piece explains why this pattern is so persistent psychologically: adult intervention is immediately rewarding because it produces visible movement, while a child's own capacity-building is slow, uneven, and full of visible failure, making it much harder for a parent to tolerate in the moment. It reframes the core parenting question from a binary 'should I help' into a more precise 'what should remain in my child's hands while I help,' and offers a specific diagnostic technique: replacing moral labels like 'my child is irresponsible' with functional questions about which specific capacity (anticipating, sequencing, remembering, recovering) is actually missing. The piece closes by naming its own central question as the ongoing test for any parental intervention: are you solving this problem for your child, or helping them become more able to solve the next version of it themselves.
points: Draws a precise distinction between an outcome (a packed backpack) and the capacity underneath it (remembering a future task, sequencing steps, noticing what's missing), arguing parents who fix only the outcome make the developmental work invisible even as the crisis resolves.

Explains the psychological asymmetry that sustains the pattern: adult intervention is immediately rewarding because it produces visible movement, while a child's own capacity-building is slow, uneven, and full of visible imperfection, making it far harder to tolerate.

Reframes intervention's core risk as ownership transfer rather than harm itself: temporary support quietly becomes the permanent family operating system, where the parent remembers, initiates, monitors, and repairs while the child waits for the next prompt.

Replaces the binary parenting question 'should I help' with a more precise operational one: 'what should remain in my child's hands while I help,' converting an all-or-nothing choice into a design question about which piece of the task to leave alone.

Supplies a concrete diagnostic reframe for common parental complaints, replacing moral labels ('my child is irresponsible,' 'my child gives up too easily') with functional questions about which specific capacity, anticipating, sequencing, remembering, or recovering, is actually missing.
quotes: Parents can work extraordinarily hard to manage a difficulty without seeing much evidence that the child is becoming more able to manage it. The reminders multiply. The supervision becomes more elaborate. The parent carries more of the mental load, while the child appears to carry less.

But an outcome and a capacity are not the same thing. The outcome may be a packed backpack. The capacity underneath it may be remembering a future task, following a sequence, noticing what is missing, or using a system without another person operating it.
Adult intervention is rewarding because it produces visible movement. A reminder gets the shoes on. Capacity develops slowly, unevenly, and often through imperfect results.

The problem is not that intervention is inherently harmful. The problem is that help can quietly change ownership. What began as temporary support becomes the way the family functions: the parent remembers, initiates, monitors, and repairs; the child waits for the next prompt.

Am I solving this problem for my child, or helping my child become more able to solve the next version of it? Good support does not require us to stand far away. It asks us to remain close without becoming the only reason the task can be done.
